(257)
Here the greatest common divisor condition selects the units. Euler's totient function φ(n) counts them; the Carmichael function gives their least common return exponent.[ref]
Modulo eight, the units are 1,3,5,7, and their squares are all congruent to one. Their multiplicative orders are 1,2,2,2, so λ(8)=2 although φ(8)=4. Modulo fifteen, the units 1,2,4,7,8,11,13,14 have multiplicative orders 1,4,2,4,4,2,4,2. For example, the powers of two return through 1,2,4,8,1. Thus λ(15)=4 although φ(15)=8; the multiplicative order of four is only two.
The three quantities are related by
λ(n)=lcm1≤a<ngcd(a,n)=1​​ordn​(a),ordn​(a)∣λ(n)∣φ(n).
(258)
A common return exponent must be a multiple of every multiplicative order, hence of their least common multiple. Conversely, that least common multiple makes every unit return to one. Lagrange's theorem makes each multiplicative order divide the group order φ(n), proving the final divisibility. The Carmichael function applies to all units at once, while the multiplicative order concerns a chosen unit.
For the prime factorization n=∏i=1r​piei​​ with distinct prime numbers pi​ and ei​≥1, the formulas are
λ(n)=lcm(λ(p1e1​​),…,λ(prer​​)),λ(pe)=pe−1(p−1)(p an odd prime),
(259)
λ(2e)=⎩⎨⎧​1,2,2e−2,​e=1,e=2,e≥3.​
(260)
These are least common multiples, rather than products: λ(15)=lcm(2,4)=4. The convention λ(1)=1 handles the trivial case separately.[ref]
The Chinese remainder theorem for unit groups explains the least common multiple: a power returns to one in every prime power component exactly when it is a multiple of each component's exponent of a finite group. For an odd prime power, the unit group is a cyclic group of group order pe−1(p−1). For e≥3, the unit group modulo 2e is a direct product of groups C2​×C2e−2​, generated by the classes of −1 and five, so its exponent of a finite group is 2e−2.[ref]
This gives a uniform reduction for modular exponentiation: for a unit a and a nonnegative integer k, reduce k modulo λ(n). For example, 21001≡2(mod15) because 1001≡1(mod4). The unit hypothesis matters: 32≡1(mod8), but 22≡1(mod8). Computing the formula assumes the prime factorization is available. The same common-exponent viewpoint explains Carmichael numbers: a composite number n passes the Fermat primality test for every unit base exactly when λ(n)∣n−1. For example, λ(561)=lcm(2,10,16)=80∣560.

Multiplicative order (ordn​(a))

Words: 852 Articles: 5
Number theory OurBigBook.com
For coprime integers a,n with n>1, the multiplicative order is the least positive integer d such that
d=ordn​(a),ad≡1(modn).
(261)
It counts the distinct powers in the cyclic subgroup generated by the congruence class of a. Thus it is an order of a group element in the unit group (Z/nZ)×.[ref]
For example, the modular exponentiation 2kmod7, starting at k=0, produces 1,2,4,1,2,4,…. The first return to one takes three steps, so ord7​(2)=3. Starting at the congruence class three and repeatedly multiplying by two instead gives 3,6,5,3,…: these are the other three units modulo seven, outside the cyclic subgroup generated by two.
Euler's theorem guarantees a return to one at exponent φ(n), where φ is Euler's totient function. Thus the multiplicative order exists for every unit.[ref] In fact,
ordn​(a)∣φ(n).
(262)
By Lagrange's theorem, the size of the cyclic subgroup divides the size of the unit group, which is Euler's totient function. For two modulo seven, this is 3∣6; the multiplicative order need not equal Euler's totient function. If a≡1(modn), its multiplicative order is one.
The coprime integers hypothesis is necessary: if ad=1+kn, any common divisor of a and n divides one. For instance, powers of two modulo eight give 1,2,4,0,0,…, with no positive-exponent return to one. This sequence eventually settles, but two has no multiplicative order modulo eight.

Decimal period from multiplicative order (ordq​(10))

Words: 391
Multiplicative order OurBigBook.com
For a reduced fraction p/q with 0<p<q, q>1, and q,10 coprime integers, its decimal representation repeats immediately after the decimal point. The shortest repeating block has length
L=ordq​(10),L∣φ(q).
(263)
Here ord denotes multiplicative order, and φ denotes Euler's totient function. Changing the numerator preserves the decimal period as long as the fraction remains reduced.[ref]
For example, long division of 1/7 gives the remainders 1,3,2,6,4,5,1, with emitted digits 1,4,2,8,5,7. Consequently
71​=0.142857,ord7​(10)=6.
(264)
Each remainder determines both the next digit and the next remainder; returning to one restarts the same six steps.
More generally, initialize long division with r0​=p. At each step, division with remainder gives
10rj−1​=qdj​+rj​,0≤dj​≤9,0≤rj​<q,
(265)
so rj​≡p10j(modq). Since p,q are coprime integers, the modular inverse of p shows that rL​=r0​ exactly when 10L≡1(modq). To see why the digit block cannot repeat sooner than the remainders, a purely repeating decimal with a block of L digits represents D/(10L−1) for an integer D. A reduced fraction p/q with that value forces q∣10L−1. Hence the shortest digit repeat and the multiplicative order coincide.
Knowing the decimal period predicts how many digits must be computed and stored: one block determines the whole repeating decimal. It also constructs the block directly. With L=ordq​(10), the integer
D=qp(10L−1)​
(266)
is the block, padded on the left with zeros to L digits. For 1/11, L=2 and D=9, so the block is 09 and 1/11=0.09. Reduction matters: 7/21=1/3=0.3 has decimal period one, whereas ord21​(10)=6.
If the reduced denominator contains prime factors two or five, ten has no multiplicative order modulo that whole denominator. Write
q=2u5vm,gcd(m,10)=1,k0​=max(u,v).
(267)
The decimal preperiod has exactly k0​ digits. If m>1, the remaining repeating decimal has decimal period ordm​(10). For instance, 28=22⋅7 gives 1/28=0.03571428: two prefix digits, then six repeating digits. If m=1, the decimal representation is a terminating decimal with exactly k0​ fractional places. We use the representation ending in zeros, rather than its alternative ending in nines; for example 1/40=0.025 terminates after three places.
A short derivation explains both cases. After k digits, multiplying the reduced fraction by 10k and discarding its integer part leaves a reduced fraction whose denominator is q/gcd(q,10k). This denominator first becomes coprime to ten at k=k0​. It then equals m, giving an immediate repeat when m>1, or an integer when m=1. The same long division argument works for positional notation in any base b≥2: for a reduced denominator q>1 coprime to b, the shortest repeating block has length ordq​(b).

Cyclic decimal divisibility

Words: 49
Multiplicative order OurBigBook.com
For an L-digit decimal integer n, moving its leading digit to the end gives a cyclic rotation c1​(n) satisfying
c1​(n)≡10n(mod10L−1).
(268)
Thus, when a modulus d divides 10L−1, every rotation has the same divisibility by d as n, up to multiplication by a power of ten.

Periodic modular exponentiation

Words: 175 Articles: 1
Multiplicative order OurBigBook.com
For a unit a modulo N, the function x↦axmodN is periodic on the integers.

Order as the exact period of modular exponentiation (ax≡ay(modn)⟺ordn​(a)∣x−y)

Words: 158
Periodic modular exponentiation OurBigBook.com
Let a,n be coprime integers with n>1, and let d=ordn​(a) be their multiplicative order. For integers x,y,
ax≡ay(modn)⟺d∣(x−y).
(269)
Negative exponents mean powers of the modular inverse of a. Thus periodic modular exponentiation has smallest positive period d, and 1,a,…,ad−1 are distinct congruence classes.[ref]
This lets a huge modular exponentiation reuse a short list: reduce its exponent modulo the multiplicative order, then look up the corresponding power. For example, 1000≡1(mod3) gives 21000≡2(mod7), while 1001≡2(mod3) gives 21001≡4(mod7). When the multiplicative order is unknown, Euler's theorem permits reduction modulo Euler's totient function, though that period may be longer. Repeated squaring remains useful when computing either the unreduced or the reduced power.
For a proof outline, multiply ax≡ay by the modular inverse of ay, leaving ax−y≡1. Apply Euclidean division to write x−y=td+r with 0≤r<d. Then ax−y≡ar; minimality of the multiplicative order forces r=0. The reverse implication follows from ad≡1. The coprime integers hypothesis enables cancellation: modulo eight, 23≡24≡0, but this repetition supplies no multiplicative order for two.

Order verification from divisors

Words: 21
Multiplicative order OurBigBook.com
To verify a candidate order r, check ar≡1 and rule out ar/q≡1 for every prime divisor q of r.

Euclidean algorithm

Words: 383 Articles: 4
Number theory OurBigBook.com
For positive integers a,b, the Euclidean algorithm repeatedly performs division with remainder: write a=qb+r with 0≤r<b, then replace (a,b) by (b,r) until the second entry is zero. The final nonzero entry is their greatest common divisor. A remainder preserves the set of common divisors: an integer divides a and b exactly when it divides b and a−qb. The positive remainders strictly decrease, so the calculation terminates.
The complete calculation for 252 and 198 is
2521985436​=1⋅198+54,=3⋅54+36,=1⋅36+18,=2⋅18+0.​
(270)
Hence gcd(252,198)=18. The fraction 252/198 reduces to 14/11 by dividing numerator and denominator by that common factor. The same remainder calculation has a geometric interpretation: remove squares from a 252-by-198 rectangle, then repeat on the remaining strip. Each division step records how many equal squares fit and the width of the new strip.
The procedure does more than test individual divisors. Each step replaces the whole common-divisor problem by a smaller equivalent one. Euclid's Book VII, Proposition 2 describes the corresponding repeated-subtraction construction; batching those subtractions into division with remainder gives the present formulation. [ref]

Extended Euclidean algorithm

Words: 81
Euclidean algorithm OurBigBook.com
The extended Euclidean algorithm also computes integers x,y satisfying ax+by=gcd(a,b), as in Bézout's identity. Back-substitution in the calculation under the Euclidean algorithm gives
18=54−36=54−(198−3⋅54)=4(252−198)−198=4⋅252−5⋅198.
(271)
Thus (x,y)=(4,−5) solves 252x+198y=18. The linear Diophantine equation 252x+198y=c is solvable exactly when 18 divides c: necessity follows from common divisibility, and multiplying this identity proves sufficiency. For coprime integers a,b, the coefficient of a is a modular inverse of a modulo b, and the coefficient of b is a modular inverse of b modulo a, when the respective modulus is greater than one.

Linear Diophantine equation

Words: 114 Articles: 2
Euclidean algorithm OurBigBook.com
A linear Diophantine equation in two variables has the form ax+by=c with integer coefficients and seeks integer solutions.

All solutions of a linear Diophantine equation ((x,y)=(x0​,y0​)+t(b/d,−a/d))

Words: 65
Linear Diophantine equation OurBigBook.com
If a,b are nonzero integers, d=gcd(a,b), and (x0​,y0​) is one solution of the linear Diophantine equation ax+by=c, then all solutions are
x=x0​+db​t,y=y0​−da​t,t∈Z.
(272)
Subtract two solutions and use the fact that a/d and b/d are coprime integers. The linear Diophantine equation solvability criterion says that a particular solution exists exactly when d divides c; the extended Euclidean algorithm constructs one. This parametrization separates existence from the complete family of answers.

Linear Diophantine equation solvability criterion

Words: 31
Linear Diophantine equation OurBigBook.com
The equation ax+by=c has an integer solution exactly when gcd(a,b) divides c. Bézout's identity proves sufficiency, while every integer linear combination of a,b is divisible by their greatest common divisor.

Sum of two squares theorem

Words: 86 Articles: 1
Number theory OurBigBook.com
A positive integer is a sum of two integer squares exactly when every prime factor congruent to 3 modulo 4 has even exponent in its prime factorization.

Congruence lattice proof of the prime sum of two squares (Λ={(a,b)∈Z2:b≡ua(modp)})

Words: 59
Sum of two squares theorem OurBigBook.com
If u2≡−1(modp), this lattice has basis (1,u),(0,p) and covolume p. The Minkowski convex body theorem applied to a disk of squared radius strictly between 4p/π and 2p gives a nonzero lattice vector with 0<a2+b2<2p. The congruence makes its squared length divisible by p, forcing a2+b2=p. The strict radius bounds avoid assuming the critical-volume form of Minkowski's theorem.
